cells.tense: A picture of what could be is alive in you and the direction is steady in your hands.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Name the direction you actually want, then put a short stretch of time into it each day for a week — enough to feel it move, not enough to wear you down.
cells.core:
You can hold something that doesn't exist yet and still aim yourself at it. What you feel when you test it against real people is the course telling you it's worth walking. What you want is the fuel, and you read it and steer. A good week looks unremarkable from outside: something half-formed shows up, you let it stay unclear, you lean toward it, and nothing needs finishing before you take the first step.

The long middle is where this usually dies, not the start. So name the direction you actually want and put a short stretch of time into it each day for a week — enough to feel it move, not enough to wear you down. Small and repeated keeps the drive alive past the point where starts go quiet, and you'll know it's working because you still want it when the week closes.
cells.sheetLine: Your read on it is clear. Keep the fire small and steady.
cells.verb: opening to what is not yet known
cells.place: where direction gets chosen and held

cells.tense: The picture will be fully finished in your head before anyone has lived a day of it.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Take one plant or a small project that's already growing and tend only that all week — water it, watch it, and let how it's actually doing set your next move.
cells.core:
The vision completes faster than the thing itself can grow. You see the whole shape early and start pulling toward it, and the gap between what you can imagine and what is actually happening reads as slowness. So more force goes in, and the pressure lands on people and plans that only needed time. Care starts costing more than it returns, and you're steering toward a future you can't write in from here.

Get back under that live edge. Take one plant or a small project that's already growing and tend only that all week: water it, watch it, and let what's actually happening set your next move. Care like that doesn't exhaust you, because the thing's own timing does the work and your hands just hold it. It also ends the charge, which is the point — people new to a real material thing often learn it faster than people who already know how it goes.
cells.sheetLine: You're finishing the future before it has been lived.

cells.tense: A choice was made some time back and you are still standing behind it.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Spend an afternoon on something you're curious about, gaining nothing from it — then settle the next call on your plate without another round of study.
cells.core:
Wanting a direction isn't the shortage here. Arriving is. You pick, and the body stays at the threshold instead of stepping through, so what you feel is watched from a step back rather than lived in. Other people's wants come through clearly enough. Your own get studied rather than entered, and a call can be refined past the point of choosing — until the refining is how you avoid showing up.

It refills through what you know. So spend an afternoon on something you're curious about, gaining nothing from it, and then settle the next call on your plate without another round of study. That knowing does the charging. You'll know you're back when a call lands and you don't reopen it, and not-knowing feels like ground to stand on rather than a reason to wait.

cells.tense: You are already moving things and will tell anyone the momentum came from somewhere else.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: After the next stretch of time on this, write what you did and what happened, in sequence, mood left out — then read the page back and count it as yours.
cells.core:
What you like is the version where you felt your way in and the shape appeared by itself. What you'll call it is instinct. Underneath sits something plainer: you looked at what was actually there, held to a method, went step by step. The reading of the room, the moment the direction got set — you'll tell people it was the mood or the timing, anything but you. So the one holding this and the one explaining it are not the same person.

Nothing needs announcing. After the next stretch of time on this, write what you did and what happened, in sequence, mood left out — then read the page back. It was you choosing, not a mood passing through. The plain record is enough to make it yours, and you won't need anyone to confirm it.
cells.sheetLine: You read the room and chose. Not the mood.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that anything in this person's life has already ended or been flooded — the record only says the capacity opens to feeling with beginner's eyes, so every cell must describe the mechanism in a moment they could recognise, not their history. The reader could reasonably say 'I don't picture things visually' — so the asks stay on acting and trying, and the sensing is named as something done, not pictured. The asks survive being wrong: each is one small thing done with wanting, not a verdict on what the person is like. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is the 'beginners get it faster' line, so it stays only in the Too Much cell where caution is the actual hazard.
